newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemalan truth commission will not name names.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalan truth commission will not name names.

text.p: Guatemala has named a high-level commission to do the dirty job of investigating the atrocities of a dirty war -- more than three decades of massacres, tortures and disappearances.

But unlike other so-called truth commissions, such as in South Africa and Argentina, Guatemala will not name names of people responsible for war crimes and the deaths or disappearances of some 140,000 people. Critics say this makes the commission's task worthless.

"In the case of (politician and newspaper publisher) Jorge Carpio, the commission would just decide that the army killed him, which all of Guatemala already knows," lawyer and activist Karen Fischer said bitterly in an interview with Reuters.
Carpio, Fischer's father-in-law, was shot to death three years ago, allegedly by civil defence patrols controlled by the army.
Fischer said the army, which has traditionally been immune to prosecution, would remain untouchable if the commission insisted on anonymity.

The government and leftist rebels, the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG), designed the truth commission during peace talks in 1994. The agreement went into effect on Dec. 29 under the terms of a comprehensive peace treaty ending the country's 30-year civil war.

The United Nations on Saturday named two Guatemalans, pedagogy professor Otilia Lux and lawyer Alfredo Balsells, to the commission. Invited by the government and the URNG, U.N. human rights expert Christian Tomuschat will chair the body.

Tomuschat, a German, monitored human rights in Guatemala for the U.N. in the early 1990s and impressed both sides of the conflict with his impartiality and his ability to master Spanish in a three-month crash course.
Tomuschat said the commission will begin in two months to delve into Guatemala's murky past.
The commission's mandate is to "objectively" report on all violence and human rights violations on both sides of the war and recommend "measures to preserve the memory of the victims."

Guatemala gained one of the worst human rights records in the Americas when the army launched a scorched-earth campaign in the 1980s, wiping out Indian villages and killing civilians targeted as potential guerrilla supporters.

Though the commission will likely blame the army for massacres and assassinations and the URNG for kidnappings and blowing up power plants, it will not name the high-ups who gave the orders or the subordinates who carried them out.
"The commission will neither individualize responsibilities nor serve as the basis for legal proceedings," Gustavo Porras, presidential adviser and peace negotiator, told Reuters.

The spirit of the commission and of the peace accords as a whole is not to identify culprits but to guarantee fundamental rights so that individuals could seek justice in the courts if they wanted, Porras said.

Porras said that spirit made this commission different from other countries where truth commissions have assigned individual blame for state-sponsored terror and violence, often working against pressure to forgive and forget.

A truth commission formed in El Salvador in 1992 did not name names publicly, but it made secret recommendations to the government for military purges. After Argentina's dirty war, a 1980s truth commission led to court convictions of military officers who later received a presidential pardon.
In South Africa, a commission has offered amnesty to people who confess their part in apartheid-era atrocities. A second body will prosecute suspects who do not confess.

Guatemala's truth squad, officially called the "Historical Clarification Commission" has six months -- with a six-month extension option -- to investigate the deaths or disappearances of an estimated 140,000 people, mostly civilians.

Investigating the entire war will be impossible for such a small commission, said Mario Polanco, director of the Mutual Support Group, a human rights group that campaigned for a larger commission to look into a smaller number of cases.
"Taking a sample, we could take on the entire period of repression. A sample means that it wouldn't just be famous cases, and it would allow going deep into the cases," Polanco told Reuters.
Polanco said the commission's mandate should be reinterpreted so that public moral sanctions will fall on guilty individuals.

The government of President Alvaro Arzu, who pushed peace talks to their conclusion last year, is vigorously promoting reconciliation among deeply divided Guatemalans, but Fischer said that shouldn't mean anonymity for the guilty.
"I'm open to forgiving, but they need to tell me who I'm forgiving," Fischer said.
